plain_english: We should also develop an easy-going temperament. Don't get too attached to whatever life fate has given you. Be ready to adapt when circumstances push you toward something new. Don't fear changes in your goals or your position in life — just avoid being fickle. Of all character flaws, fickleness is the most destructive to peace of mind. Stubbornness makes you anxious and miserable (though Fortune sometimes forces stubborn people to give in). But fickleness is even worse because it never lets you rest. Both extremes — never changing anything and being dissatisfied with everything — are enemies of inner peace.
original_excerpt: Moreover, we ought to cultivate an easy temper, and not become over fond of the lot which fate has assigned to us, but transfer ourselves to whatever other condition chance may lead us to, and fear no alteration, either in our purposes or our position in life, provided that we do not become subject to caprice, which of all vices is the most hostile to repose: for obstinacy, from which Fortune often wrings some concession, must needs be anxious and unhappy, but caprice, which can never restrain itself, must be more so. Both of these qualities, both that of altering nothing, and that of being dissatisfied with everything, are energies to repose.

plain_english: Your mind should always turn away from focusing on outside things and look inward instead. Let it trust itself, find joy in itself, and admire its own achievements. Avoid other people's business as much as possible, and focus on yourself. Don't feel crushed by losses. Try to see even bad luck in a positive light. Zeno, the founder of our philosophy, heard that a shipwreck had destroyed all his property. His response? "Fortune is telling me to pursue philosophy with less baggage."
original_excerpt: The mind ought in all cases to be called away from the contemplation of external things to that of itself: let it confide in itself, rejoice in itself, admire its own works; avoid as far as may be those of others, and devote itself to itself; let it not feel losses, and put a good construction even upon misfortunes. Zeno, the chief of our school, when he heard the news of a shipwreck, in which all his property had been lost, remarked, "Fortune bids me follow philosophy in lighter marching order."

plain_english: A tyrant threatened to kill Theodorus and leave his body unburied. Theodorus replied, "Do whatever makes you happy. You can spill my blood if you want — that's up to you. But as for burial, you'd have to be an idiot to think I care whether I rot above ground or underground."
original_excerpt: A tyrant threatened Theodorus with death, and even with want of burial. "You are able to please yourself," he answered, "my half pint of blood is in your power: for, as for burial, what a fool you must be if you suppose that I care whether I rot above ground or under it."

plain_english: Julius Kanus was a man of extraordinary greatness. Even the fact that he lived in our terrible times doesn't stop us from admiring him. He had a long argument with Gaius. As he was leaving, that tyrant said to him, "Don't fool yourself with false hope. I've ordered you to be executed." Kanus replied, "Thank you, most excellent prince." I'm not sure what he meant. Several explanations come to mind. Was he being sarcastic to show Gaius how cruel he was — that death had become a mercy? Was he mocking the emperor's well-known madness? Even people whose children were killed and property seized used to thank Gaius. Or did Kanus welcome death because he saw it as freedom? Whatever he meant, it was a brave answer.
original_excerpt: Julius Kanus, a man of peculiar greatness, whom even the fact of his having been born in this century does not prevent our admiring, had a long dispute with Gaius, and when as he was going away that Phalaris of a man said to him, "That you may not delude yourself with any foolish hopes, I have ordered you to be executed," he answered, "I thank you, most excellent prince." I am not sure what he meant: for many ways of explaining his conduct occur to me. Did he wish to be reproachful, and to show him how great his cruelty must be if death became a kindness? or did he upbraid him with his accustomed insanity? for even those whose children were put to death, and whose goods were confiscated, used to thank him: or was it that he willingly received death, regarding it as freedom? Whatever he meant, it was a magnanimous answer.

plain_english: Someone might say, "After this, Gaius could have let him live." But Kanus wasn't worried about that. Everyone knew how reliably Gaius followed through on execution orders. Can you believe that Kanus spent the ten days before his death without any despair? It's amazing how calmly he spoke and acted. How peaceful he was. He was playing checkers when the centurion came to collect the condemned prisoners. When called, Kanus counted his pieces and said to his opponent, "Don't lie after I'm dead and claim you were winning." Then he turned to the centurion and said, "You can witness that I'm ahead by one piece." Do you think Kanus was just playing a game on that board? No — he was playing with death itself.
original_excerpt: Some one may say, "After this Gaius might have let him live." Kanus had no fear of this: the good faith with which Gaius carried out such orders as these was well known. Will you believe that he passed the ten intervening days before his execution without the slightest despondency? it is marvellous how that man spoke and acted, and how peaceful he was. He was playing at draughts when the centurion in charge of a number of those who where going to be executed bade him join them: on the summons he counted his men and said to his companion, "Mind you do not tell a lie after my death, and say that you won;" then, turning to the centurion, he said "You will bear me witness that I am one man ahead of him." Do you think that Kanus played upon that draught-board? nay, he played with it.

plain_english: His friends were sad about losing such a great man. "Why are you upset?" he asked them. "You spend your time wondering if souls live on after death. Well, I'm about to find out." Right up to the end, he kept searching for truth. He even used his own death as a chance to learn something new. His philosophy teacher walked with him to his execution. When they got close to the hill where they made daily sacrifices to Caesar, the teacher asked, "What are you thinking about now, Kanus? What's going through your mind?" Kanus replied, "I've decided to use this moment — the fastest moment of all — to see if my spirit will notice itself leaving my body." He even promised that if he learned anything, he would somehow visit his friends and tell them what it's like for souls after death.
original_excerpt: His friends were sad at being about to lose so great a man: "Why," asked he, "are you sorrowful? you are enquiring whether our souls are immortal, but I shall presently know." Nor did he up to the very end cease his search after truth, and raised arguments upon the subject of his own death. His own teacher of philosophy accompanied him, and they were not far from the hill on which the daily sacrifice to Caesar our god was offered, when he said, "What are you thinking of now, Kanus? or what are your ideas?" "I have decided," answered Kanus, "at that most swiftly-passing moment of all to watch whether the spirit will be conscious of the act of leaving the body." He promised, too, that if he made any discoveries, he would come round to his friends and tell them what the condition of the souls of the departed might be.

plain_english: Here was peace in the middle of chaos. Here was a soul that deserved to live forever — one who used his own suffering as proof of what he believed. Even at death's door, he kept experimenting with his last breaths. He didn't just keep learning until he died. He learned something from death itself. No one has lived the philosopher's life more completely. I won't quickly move on from talking about such a great man — one who deserves our respect. I will pass your memory down to future generations, you most noble heart, greatest among all the many victims of Gaius.
original_excerpt: Here was peace in the very midst of the storm: here was a soul worthy of eternal life, which used its own fate as a proof of truth, which when at the last step of life experimented upon his fleeting breath, and did not merely continue to learn until he died, but learned something even from death itself. No man has carried the life of a philosopher further. I will not hastily leave the subject of a great man, and one who deserves to be spoken of with respect: I will hand thee down to all posterity, thou most noble heart, chief among the many victims of Gaius.
